Portable electric breast pumps
A portable breast pump on this page is an electric breast pump with a built-in battery. You charge it, then pump without a wall socket. These portable electric breast pumps are compact enough for a bag: motor in the cup, or a hospital-strength motor you carry outside the cup.
Portable means battery, so you’re not plugged in while you pump. Every electric breast pump here works that way.
Want the motor in the cup and no tubes? Choose an all-in-one electric. Want the motor off your chest? Choose V1 Pro or V2 Pro.
If you want a tube-free cup in your bra — including hands-free or wireless — go to the Wearable collection . This page stays with electric and portable.
Which electric breast pump is right for y

ou?
There isn’t one best electric breast pump. It depends what you need it for: everyday pumping, a portable kit with a charging case, warmth and massage, or a hospital-strength motor off your chest.
M5 Smart is the everyday electric breast pump for most UK mums: an app, and suction up to −285 mmHg. Start here for a portable electric with a phone app.
230 g · built-in battery, about 6 sessions · under 48 dB · double or single · cup in a bra or a bag
Air 1 is the portable electric with a charging case for longer days out, and a 61 mm cup. Choose it if you want extra charge away from a wall socket.
260 g · charging case, up to 15 sessions · 45 dB or under · cup in a bra or a bag
Wellness 1 warms the cup and adds massage with the suction rhythm, with three warmth levels at 37°C, 39°C and 41°C. App control, so you can adjust warmth and massage from your phone.
320 g · about 10 sessions, about 6 with warmth · under 50 dB · cup in a bra or a bag
Hospital-strength, motor off the chest
V1 Pro is the hospital-strength electric if you want the motor off your chest: 15 levels, up to −300 mmHg, for longer sessions at home. V2 Pro is the same type with a 127 g motor if you want a lighter unit.
240 g motor · built-in battery, about 9 sessions · motor in a bag · V2 Pro motor 127 g, under 48 dB
All-in-one electric means the motor sits in the cup, with no tubes. Hospital-strength electric means the motor sits outside. Then check suction, battery, weight, noise and where you carry it.
About 10 sessions; about 6 with warmth
Hospital-strength, motor outside
Electric vs manual breast pumps
Choose an electric breast pump if you pump most days, you’re going back to work, or you want both sides done in one session. A motor does the squeezing for you, and most have a let-down mode then an expression mode, so it takes less time. You pay more, and you charge it.
Choose a manual pump if you only express now and then, or want a quiet spare with no charging. It’s slower if you need a lot of milk every day.
Most electric kits are doubles, so you can express both sides in one session and cut the time. If feeding isn’t going well, speak to your midwife or health visitor.
Bags, bras and a bottle washer
Once you switch the motor off, you still need to store the milk, keep the cups in place, and wash the parts.
Use breast milk storage bags to label and freeze milk flat. Follow NHS guidance on how long milk keeps. A storage jug is useful at home if you prefer to pour milk together before you bag it.
A pumping bra holds the cups in place while you pump. An ordinary stretchy bra can work; a pumping bra is more likely to stay put.
A bottle washer washes and sterilises pump parts in one go, so you’re not facing a sink of parts after every session. It is faster than cleaning breast pump parts by hand. Add a washing block if you want the detergent measured for you.
How to choose a portable electric breast pump
Check the grams if you’ll carry it. M5 Smart is 230 g. Air 1 is 260 g. Wellness 1 is 320 g. V2 Pro’s motor is 127 g if you want the motor off your chest and lighter in a bag.
These charge with USB-C, then run on battery. M5 Smart is about 6 sessions. Air 1’s charging case goes up to 15. Warmth on Wellness 1 uses more battery, about 6 sessions instead of 10.
A double electric kit expresses both sides in one session. Buy a single only if you usually pump one side, or you want a spare. M5 Smart is sold as double or single.
Quieter matters at work or at night. M9 is 42 dB or under. Air 1 and S9 Pro are 45 dB or under. M5 Smart and V2 Pro are under 48 dB.
An all-in-one cup can sit in a bra or go in a bag. On V1 Pro and V2 Pro the motor goes in a bag, off your chest. For a tube-free in-bra pump, including hands-free or wireless, see the Wearable collection .
When you know which type you want, check suction, battery and breast pump price .
What is an electric breast pump?
An electric breast pump uses a motor to express milk, so you’re not squeezing a handle. You can get

a portable electric with the motor in the cup, or a hospital-strength pump where the motor sits outside.
Which electric breast pump is best?
There isn’t one best pump for every mum. Most people start with M5 Smart for everyday use. Choose Air 1 if you want a portable kit with a charging case. Choose Wellness 1 if you want in-cup warmth and massage. Choose V1 Pro if you want a stronger motor off your chest.
Is an electric breast pump portable?
Yes. Every electric breast pump on this page has a built-in battery, so you’re not plugged into the wall while you pump. Portable here means battery-powered and compact enough to carry: at home, at work, or out. It is not the same thing as a wearable pump.
Can I use a portable electric pump while travelling?
Yes. Charge it before you leave. A portable electric breast pump runs on its battery, and these kits charge by USB-C from a wall plug, a laptop or a power bank. For several sessions away from a socket, Air 1’s charging case lasts longest on this page, up to 15 sessions. Pack it in your cabin bag and check your airline’s rules for lithium batteries before you fly.
What’s the difference between portable and wearable?
Portable means the pump runs on a battery, so you’re not tied to a socket. Wearable, on this site, means a tube-free in-bra cup, including hands-free and wireless. Those sit on the Wearable collection . A pump can be portable and still be the hospital-strength type, with the motor in a bag rather than in the cup.
What’s the difference between the two types of electric pump?
The difference is where the motor sits. One type has the motor in the cup: no tubes. That’s M5 Smart, Air 1, Wellness 1, M6, M9, S12 Pro Quick and S9 Pro. The other type keeps the motor outside on a short tube. That’s V1 Pro and V2 Pro — hospital-strength, with the motor off your chest. Choose the no-tube type if you want to move around with nothing hanging off you. Choose V1 Pro or V2 Pro if you’d rather keep a stronger motor off your chest.
What is a hospital-strength electric pump?
Hospital-strength means a stronger motor that sits outside, off your chest. On this page that’s V1 Pro and V2 Pro. They are electric pumps you can still carry, with the motor in a bag. If you want a tube-free cup in your bra — including hands-free or wireless — see the Wearable collection.
Should I get an electric or a manual pump?
Go electric if you pump most days, you’re going back to work, or you want both sides done in one go. A manual pump is fine if you only express now and then, and you want something quiet with no charging.
Can I pump both sides at once?
Yes. Most electric kits do both sides together, which is the usual choice if you express from both breasts. A few are also sold as a single — only pick that if you usually pump one side, or you want a spare.
Do I need a pumping bra or storage bags?
You can pump without them, but most mums who express every day end up wanting both. A pumping bra holds the cups in place while you pump. Bags let you label and freeze milk for later.
How should I store expressed milk?
Follow the NHS. They currently say fridge for up to 8 days at 4°C or lower, and freezer at −18°C or lower for up to 6 months. Some NHS pages also allow up to 6 hours at room temperature. Check the NHS expressing page for the latest.
Can an electric pump help with engorgement?
It can take the pressure off if you feel uncomfortably full. If you think you have mastitis, feeding hurts, or baby is not getting milk, talk to your midwife or health visitor.
